question.text:
Suppose we wish to prove the following statement using mathematical induction:

\[ \sum_{i=2}^n i(i-1) = \dfrac 13 n(n-1)(n+1) \]

A proof template is outlined below. Fill in the missing statements.
question.explanation:
To prove a statement using induction, we use the following framework:

  • Step 1: Base Case

  • Step 2: Inductive Hypothesis

  • Step 3: Inductive Step

  • Step 4: Conclusion

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

\[ \sum_{i=2}^n i(i-1) = \dfrac 13 n(n-1)(n+1) \]

We start by proving the so-called base case, $P(2).$ To do this, we substitute $n=2$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side.

In our case, this gives the following:

Base Case: We first prove that our statement is true for the base case $n=2.$ \begin{align*} \sum_{i=2}^2 i(i-1) = \dfrac 13 (2)(2-1)(2+1) \end{align*}

Proving that the base case is true is usually straightforward. We simply calculate the left-hand and right-hand sides independently and show they're equal.

Next, we write down our inductive hypothesis. We assume that $P(k)$ is true for some $n=k\geq 2.$ To do this, we simply replace $n$ with $k$ in our original statement $P(n).$

In our case, this gives the following:

Inductive Hypothesis: We assume that for some $n=k\geq 2,$ we have \[\sum_{i=2}^k i(i-1) = \dfrac 13 k (k-1)(k+1).\]

Due to the base case, we already know that the statement is true for some value of $k,$ namely $k=2,$ so this assumption is valid.

Then, we move onto the inductive step: We must show that $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1).$ We start by writing down $P(k+1).$

Inductive Step: We're required to prove that \begin{align*} \sum_{i=2}^{k+1} i(i-1) &= \dfrac 13 (k+1) \left((k+1)-1\right)\left((k+1)+1\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 13 k(k+1)(k+2). \end{align*}

The inductive step is where most of the work lies. The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of this equation using the inductive hypothesis and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

Once we've shown that $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1),$ the proof is complete, and we state our conclusion.

Conclusion: Therefore, $\displaystyle\sum_{i=2}^n i(i-1) = \dfrac 13 n (n-1)(n+1)$ for all $n\geq 2.$

question.explanation:
We need to express the summation $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k).$

Let $a_i$ for $i\geq 1$ be a sequence, and let $S(k)$ denote the sum of the first $k$ terms.

\[ S(k) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i \]

We can always express $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k)$ by writing the last term on its own, as follows:

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} a_i = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i\right) + a_{k+1}. \]

In our case, we have $a_i = i(i-1)(i+1).$ Therefore, \begin{align*} a_{k+1} = (k+1)(k+1-1)(k+1+1) = k(k+1)(k+2). \end{align*}

Hence,

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} i(i-1)(i+1) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} i(i-1)(i+1) \right) + \big( k(k+1)(k+2) \big), \]

which we can write as \[ S(k+1) = S(k) + k(k+1)(k+2). \]

exampleAnswers.title: Proving Sums of Series Using Induction

question.explanation:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1), P(2), P(3), \ldots,$ where

  • $P(1)$ is true, and

  • $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$ for every $k \in \mathbb N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n \in \mathbb N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following: \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \dfrac{1}{3^i} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \]

We start by proving the so-called base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n = 1$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

Base Case: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n = 1.$ For the left-hand side, we have \begin{align*} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^1 \dfrac{1}{3^i} = \dfrac{1}{3}, \end{align*} and for the right-hand side, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}. \end{align*} Thus, our statement is true for $n = 1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n = k \geq 1.$

Due to the base case, we already know that the statement is true for some value of $k,$ namely $k = 1,$ so this assumption is valid.

Inductive Hypothesis: We assume that for some $n = k \geq 1,$ we have \[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \dfrac{1}{3^i} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^k}\right). \]

We must show that $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the so-called inductive step, so let's write that, too.

Inductive Step: We're required to prove that \[ \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \dfrac{1}{3^i} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^{k+1}}\right). \qquad\qquad (\ast) \]

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(\ast)$ using the inductive hypothesis and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving sums of finite series using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to write the last term on its own, as follows: \[ \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} a_i = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i\right) + a_{k+1} \]

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write \[\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \dfrac{1}{3^i} =\displaystyle \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} \dfrac{1}{3^i} \right) + \dfrac{1}{3^{k+1}}. \] By the inductive hypothesis, we have \begin{align*} \displaystyle \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} \dfrac{1}{3^i} \right) + \dfrac{1}{3^{k+1}} & = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^k}\right) + \dfrac{1}{3^{k+1}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3^k} + \dfrac{1}{3^{k+1}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3^k}\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3^k}\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3^k}\left(\dfrac{1}{2 \cdot 3}\right)\\[5pt] %& = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3^{k+1}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^{k+1}}\right), \end{align*} as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(\ast)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction, $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \dfrac{1}{3^i} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)$ is true for all $n \geq 1.$
